trial.ground_truth: Inventory executes pg_sleep(1.2) before catalog SQL
trial.predicted_root_cause: inventory-service's GET /products handler issues an unconditional SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) against Postgres on every request, adding a fixed ~1.2s stall. This is not a genuinely slow query: pg_stat_statements shows the real products SELECT (SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT $1) at mean_exec_time 0.108ms, while SELECT pg_sleep has mean_exec_time 1202ms. Live pg_stat_activity shows multiple 'active' SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) sessions with application_name=inventory-service. inventory-service /products logs are all HTTP 200 at ~1206-1214ms (no errors). The stall sits on the order-service /checkout critical path: a trace shows order-service's GET http://inventory-service:8000/products client span lasting 1.21s, which propagates up so that gateway, order-service and inventory-service all plateau near 1.2s p95. Redis and Kafka are healthy (TTL 30; consumer lag 0), and payment/user/notification remain fast, ruling them out.

regression_risks: Diagnosis relies on application_name=inventory-service attribution; if multiple code paths or jobs share that connection label, the sleep call site is inferred, not proven from source (inventory-service not in allowlisted scope; repository searches returned no matches).

The source line issuing pg_sleep is not captured; removing the wrong call or a cached/alternate code path could leave the stall present, and reintroducing a load-simulation sleep without a non-production gate risks recurrence on the /checkout critical path.

Redis catalog_ttl fell to 5 in a later snapshot (E-b2f75ac765bf46b6) and pool usage_ms grew monotonically (E-4b49b7cabf1141f2 -> E-b295ceb88c3342fc), suggesting unverified cache/pool behavior that could mask a returning latency regression.
critic_result.test_sufficiency: Sufficient to confirm the pg_sleep(1.2) mechanism (trace spans, active PgSleep sessions, matching log/HTTP durations, and mean_exec stats). Insufficient as a controlled fix validation: no source-level patch, allowlisted repo searches returned no matches, before/after windows are non-identical, and the post-change snapshot shows TTL 5 with growing pool usage_ms. NO_CODE_PATCH; recovery was operator-observed, not an AI-verified repair.
critic_result.verification_summary: The pg_sleep(1.2) stall attached to the inventory-service /products path is independently corroborated by multiple sources. (1) Two DB activity snapshots show 'active' SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event=PgSleep, application_name=inventory-service (E-041af48eda94420f, E-8e6072ae7bf94f16), while the real products SELECT is idle. (2) A trace directly contains a postgresql span with db.statement 'SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)' under psycopg instrumentation (E-f318d90c32e84a9c), placing the sleep on the request path, not merely adjacent. (3) Logs: every inventory /products entry is HTTP 200 with duration ~1206-1214ms (E-b3e93f3dbda64027), matching the sleep duration to within ~1%. (4) Metrics show gateway/inventory/order plateauing near ~1.2s while payment/user stay <10ms in the same windows (E-9d495c1f0b4e4f71, E-3e8d0e5a22f44a2b). (5) DB statement stats show pg_sleep mean_exec ~1202ms vs products SELECT ~0.108ms, with equal one-second call deltas of 3/3, consistent with one sleep per products call. Note: the diagnosis labels the single 1.2s delay as the root cause; the observed HTTP durations (~1206-1237ms) slightly exceed 1.2s, so additional sub-100ms overhead exists on the path but is not the dominant factor. This was a NO_CODE_PATCH, operator-run restoration; no AI patch was applied and recovery is observational only. The 'before/after' the operator reports actually straddles different incident phases: a later snapshot (E-b295ceb88c3342fc) still shows inventory-service SELECT 1 with no pg_sleep, yet Redis catalog TTL is 5 and pool usage_ms is rising (~639s), so the recovery is not a clean controlled A/B and the sleep may simply have been toggled off between phases rather than structurally removed.

alternative_explanations: The ~1.2s plateau could be a shared client/pool contention artifact: inventory-service pool-stats show requests_wait_ms 12853 and usage_ms growing monotonically across snapshots (E-4b49b7cabf1141f2, E-c087f231eceb4c26), so queueing could contribute; however the exact 1.2s match to pg_sleep and the product query's 0.108ms mean make the sleep the dominant term, not the pool.

The 'before/after' latency drop (1.2s -> ~5-71ms) is not a controlled AI experiment: snapshots span differing windows, catalog_ttl drops 30->5->(later) with hits/misses shifting, and there is no explicit code revert, so improvement could reflect the injected stall being switched off rather than the fix being validated.

Observed HTTP durations (~1206-1237ms) slightly exceed the configured 1.2s sleep, indicating some non-sleep overhead (pool waits/connection setup) that the diagnosis does not fully account for; this does not overturn the dominant cause but leaves a residual unexplained term.

initial_hypotheses: Inventory-service GET /products path is the bottleneck: a 1.2s latency plateau at inventory-service is propagated up through order-service and gateway on the /checkout critical path.
Postgres is contended by inventory-service: active PgSleep(1.2) sessions and high cumulative request_wait_ms (12853) indicate DB-side waiting, not HTTP errors.
Redis dependency shared by order/inventory/gateway/payment may add latency, since cache health cannot be established from HTTP health signals.
Latency is load/stall-driven rather than error-driven, since all services report 0% HTTP errors and healthy health checks despite elevated p50/p95.

llm_findings: inventory-service GET /products runs SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) per request (active PgSleep sessions, application_name=inventory-service), while the real products SELECT is 0.108ms — a deliberate fixed DB stall, not query slowness.
A real trace span (order-service -> GET http://inventory-service:8000/products) lasts 1.21s, exactly matching the plateau seen at inventory-service, order-service and gateway.
inventory-service /products logs are all HTTP 200 at ~1206-1214ms with zero errors, so this is a latency/liveness issue, not an error-driven outage.

Redis (TTL 30, cumulative counters) and Kafka (consumer lag 0) are healthy; payment-service (~5ms) and user-service (~1.3ms) are unaffected — ruling out cache, queue, pool-exhaustion and payment paths.
Postgres pool wait on inventory-service (requests_wait_ms) is collateral of the sleep holding connections, not the cause; DB query latency for products is sub-millisecond.
arguments.recommended_fix: Remove the unconditional SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) from the inventory-service /products handler so the endpoint returns in sub-millisecond query time. If a load-simulation stall is required, gate it behind an explicit non-production config flag and never on the /checkout critical path. Re-verify: pg_stat_statements pg_sleep calls_growth should drop to ~0 and inventory/order/gateway p95 should return to <50ms. No pricing/order-service code change is applicable (pricing is a function in order-service and is not implicated).
arguments.reasoning_summary: Independent sources triangulate: (1) DB — pg_stat_statements SELECT pg_sleep mean_exec=1202ms (378->483 calls) with active PgSleep(1.2) sessions tagged inventory-service, while the products query is 0.108ms; a 1s delta shows both advancing 3 calls, i.e. one sleep per products request. (2) Traces — a real span shows order-service -> GET http://inventory-service:8000/products lasting 1,214,906us, matching the ~1.2s plateau. (3) Logs — every inventory /products entry is HTTP 200 at ~1206-1214ms, no errors. (4) Metrics — gateway/order/inventory all plateau ~1.2s p95 while payment/user/notification stay <10ms, consistent with a single shared downstream stall rather than independent faults. Redis cumulative counters and Kafka lag=0 exclude cache/queue as the driver. The stall is a deliberate injected DB wait inside the /products path, so the products SELECT itself is healthy.

deterministic_signals.explanation: gateway ~1.2s p95 latency is a propagated symptom: the trace shows the slow leaf is the order-service->inventory-service /products call (1.21s), and gateway only aggregates it.
inventory-service is the origin: /products logs 1206-1214ms with HTTP 200, and pg activity shows active SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) sessions from inventory-service, matching the 1.2s span.
order-service ~1.24s p95 is the caller retrying/waiting on its inventory-service GET /products span; it is an upstream symptom of the same stall, not an independent fault.

remaining_uncertainty: inventory-service source is outside allowlisted scope, so the exact pg_sleep call site/line in the /products handler could not be cited directly; attribution relies on application_name=inventory-service in pg activity and the matching 1.2s plateau.
Whether the pg_sleep is unconditional for every call or rate-limited could not be distinguished (call deltas show 3 sleeps per 1s alongside 3 products queries, implying per-request).

Redis keyspace hits/misses are cumulative totals, so cache effectiveness in this window is not directly measurable; it is excluded as a driver only because latency matches the DB sleep exactly and Redis TTL is healthy.

(2) A trace directly contains a postgresql span with db.statement 'SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)' under psycopg instrumentation (E-f318d90c32e84a9c), placing the sleep on the request path, not merely adjacent. (3) Logs: every inventory /products entry is HTTP 200 with duration ~1206-1214ms (E-b3e93f3dbda64027), matching the sleep duration to within ~1%. (4) Metrics show gateway/inventory/order plateauing near ~1.2s while payment/user stay <10ms in the same windows (E-9d495c1f0b4e4f71, E-3e8d0e5a22f44a2b). (5) DB statement stats show pg_sleep mean_exec ~1202ms vs products SELECT ~0.108ms, with equal one-second call deltas of 3/3, consistent with one sleep per products call. Note: the diagnosis labels the single 1.2s delay as the root cause; the observed HTTP durations (~1206-1237ms) slightly exceed 1.2s, so additional sub-100ms overhead exists on the path but is not the dominant factor. This was a NO_CODE_PATCH, operator-run restoration; no AI patch was applied and recovery is observational only. The 'before/after' the operator reports actually straddles different incident phases: a later snapshot (E-b295ceb88c3342fc) still shows inventory-service SELECT 1 with no pg_sleep, yet Redis catalog TTL is 5 and pool usage_ms is rising (~639s), so the recovery is not a clean controlled A/B and the sleep may simply have been toggled off between phases rather than structurally removed.

payload.summary: Independent sources triangulate: (1) DB — pg_stat_statements SELECT pg_sleep mean_exec=1202ms (378->483 calls) with active PgSleep(1.2) sessions tagged inventory-service, while the products query is 0.108ms; a 1s delta shows both advancing 3 calls, i.e. one sleep per products request. (2) Traces — a real span shows order-service -> GET http://inventory-service:8000/products lasting 1,214,906us, matching the ~1.2s plateau. (3) Logs — every inventory /products entry is HTTP 200 at ~1206-1214ms, no errors. (4) Metrics — gateway/order/inventory all plateau ~1.2s p95 while payment/user/notification stay <10ms, consistent with a single shared downstream stall rather than independent faults. Redis cumulative counters and Kafka lag=0 exclude cache/queue as the driver. The stall is a deliberate injected DB wait inside the /products path, so the products SELECT itself is healthy.

diagnosis.root_cause: inventory-service's GET /products handler issues an unconditional SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) against Postgres on every request, adding a fixed ~1.2s stall. This is not a genuinely slow query: pg_stat_statements shows the real products SELECT (SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT $1) at mean_exec_time 0.108ms, while SELECT pg_sleep has mean_exec_time 1202ms. Live pg_stat_activity shows multiple 'active' SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) sessions with application_name=inventory-service. inventory-service /products logs are all HTTP 200 at ~1206-1214ms (no errors). The stall sits on the order-service /checkout critical path: a trace shows order-service's GET http://inventory-service:8000/products client span lasting 1.21s, which propagates up so that gateway, order-service and inventory-service all plateau near 1.2s p95. Redis and Kafka are healthy (TTL 30; consumer lag 0), and payment/user/notification remain fast, ruling them out.
diagnosis.recommended_fix: Remove the unconditional SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) from the inventory-service /products handler so the endpoint returns in sub-millisecond query time. If a load-simulation stall is required, gate it behind an explicit non-production config flag and never on the /checkout critical path. Re-verify: pg_stat_statements pg_sleep calls_growth should drop to ~0 and inventory/order/gateway p95 should return to <50ms. No pricing/order-service code change is applicable (pricing is a function in order-service and is not implicated).

critic.verification_summary: The pg_sleep(1.2) stall attached to the inventory-service /products path is independently corroborated by multiple sources. (1) Two DB activity snapshots show 'active' SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event=PgSleep, application_name=inventory-service (E-041af48eda94420f, E-8e6072ae7bf94f16), while the real products SELECT is idle. (2) A trace directly contains a postgresql span with db.statement 'SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)' under psycopg instrumentation (E-f318d90c32e84a9c), placing the sleep on the request path, not merely adjacent. (3) Logs: every inventory /products entry is HTTP 200 with duration ~1206-1214ms (E-b3e93f3dbda64027), matching the sleep duration to within ~1%. (4) Metrics show gateway/inventory/order plateauing near ~1.2s while payment/user stay <10ms in the same windows (E-9d495c1f0b4e4f71, E-3e8d0e5a22f44a2b). (5) DB statement stats show pg_sleep mean_exec ~1202ms vs products SELECT ~0.108ms, with equal one-second call deltas of 3/3, consistent with one sleep per products call. Note: the diagnosis labels the single 1.2s delay as the root cause; the observed HTTP durations (~1206-1237ms) slightly exceed 1.2s, so additional sub-100ms overhead exists on the path but is not the dominant factor. This was a NO_CODE_PATCH, operator-run restoration; no AI patch was applied and recovery is observational only. The 'before/after' the operator reports actually straddles different incident phases: a later snapshot (E-b295ceb88c3342fc) still shows inventory-service SELECT 1 with no pg_sleep, yet Redis catalog TTL is 5 and pool usage_ms is rising (~639s), so the recovery is not a clean controlled A/B and the sleep may simply have been toggled off between phases rather than structurally removed.

alternative_explanations: The ~1.2s plateau could be a shared client/pool contention artifact: inventory-service pool-stats show requests_wait_ms 12853 and usage_ms growing monotonically across snapshots (E-4b49b7cabf1141f2, E-c087f231eceb4c26), so queueing could contribute; however the exact 1.2s match to pg_sleep and the product query's 0.108ms mean make the sleep the dominant term, not the pool.

The 'before/after' latency drop (1.2s -> ~5-71ms) is not a controlled AI experiment: snapshots span differing windows, catalog_ttl drops 30->5->(later) with hits/misses shifting, and there is no explicit code revert, so improvement could reflect the injected stall being switched off rather than the fix being validated.

Observed HTTP durations (~1206-1237ms) slightly exceed the configured 1.2s sleep, indicating some non-sleep overhead (pool waits/connection setup) that the diagnosis does not fully account for; this does not overturn the dominant cause but leaves a residual unexplained term.
